title: Waiting for two heads in a row
objectives: Find the expected flips until a pattern appears with first-step analysis.

screens.title: The first head
screens.prose: Flip a fair coin until the first head. The chain has two states: no head yet, and done.

state.caption: States are the part of the pattern built so far. Each flip is H or T with chance $\tfrac12$.

screens.question: How many flips do you expect to make?

hints.text: Each flip is a head with chance $\tfrac12$.
A tail loops back to the start.
A geometric wait: $1/\tfrac12 = 2$.

feedback.correct: A chance of $\tfrac12$ per flip takes $1/\tfrac12 = 2$ flips on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each flip succeeds with chance $\tfrac12$.

byKey.one: One flip is enough only half the time. A tail costs another try.
byKey.half: That is the chance per flip. The wait is its reciprocal.

explain.text: Each flip is a head with chance $\tfrac12$, so this is a geometric wait of $2$ flips. A tail leaves you where you started.

screens.title: Head then tail
screens.prose: Now flip until you see a head followed at once by a tail, HT. The chain tracks how much of HT you have built: its **state**.

state.caption: States are the part of the pattern built so far. Each flip is H or T with chance $\tfrac12$.

screens.question: How many flips do you expect until HT?

hints.text: How long until the first H?
Once at H, a head keeps you there.
Wait 2 flips for H, then 2 more for T: $2 + 2 = 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Wait for the H, then wait for the T.

byKey.three: You allowed one flip for the T. A tail comes with chance $\tfrac12$, so it takes 2 flips on average.
byKey.six: At state H, an extra head keeps you at H. It never sends you back to the start.

explain.text: Reaching H takes 2 flips on average. At H, a head keeps you at H and a tail finishes, so 2 more flips. The total is 4.

screens.title: Two heads
screens.prose: Now wait for HH. At state H a tail sends you back to the start. Let $E_0$ and $E_H$ be the expected flips to finish. Condition on the next flip: $$\begin{aligned} E_0 &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_0 \\ E_H &= 1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 + \tfrac12 E_0 \end{aligned}$$

state.caption: States are the part of the pattern built so far. Each flip is H or T with chance $\tfrac12$.

screens.question: Solve the pair and fill in the table.

hints.text: One flip is spent, then you start afresh from where it lands.
From H, a tail sends you back to the start.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $E_H = 1 + \tfrac12 E_0$ into the first equation.

byKey.r0c1: From H, half the time you finish in 1 flip and half the time you restart: $E_H = 1 + \tfrac12 E_0$.

explain.text: This is **first-step analysis**: one flip is spent, then the wait starts afresh from the state it reaches. Here $E_0 = 6$ and $E_H = 4$. The tail from H back to the start is what costs the extra flips.

screens.title: Same chance, same wait?
screens.prose: A candidate argues: any two flips show HH with chance $\tfrac14$, and HT with chance $\tfrac14$ too. So the two patterns take equally long to appear.

state.caption: States are the part of the pattern built so far. Each flip is H or T with chance $\tfrac12$.

screens.question: Which is right?

options.text: HT takes 4 flips on average and HH takes 6

options.why: Equal chances per pair of flips do not give equal waits. A failed HH throws away its head; a failed HT keeps it.
HT never goes back to the start once it has an H, so it is quicker than HH.

options.text: HH is quicker, because heads come in streaks
options.why: Fair flips do not streak. Each flip is a head with chance $\tfrac12$, whatever came before.

hints.text: Look at state H in each chain.
For HT a head keeps you at H; for HH a tail sends you to the start.
HT: $2 + 2 = 4$. HH: you found $E_0 = 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what a wrong flip does at state H for each pattern.

byKey.b: You took equal chances to mean equal waits. HH occurrences overlap, as in HHH, so they come in clumps with longer gaps between.

explain.text: Both patterns appear equally often in a long run of flips. But HH overlaps itself: HHH holds two of them, so they clump and the gaps between clumps are longer. A wrong flip at H costs HH everything and costs HT nothing.

screens.title: Three heads
screens.prose: Wait for HHH. A tail from any state sends you to the start: $$\begin{aligned} E_0 &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_0 \\ E_H &= 1 + \tfrac12 E_{HH} + \tfrac12 E_0 \\ E_{HH} &= 1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 + \tfrac12 E_0 \end{aligned}$$

state.caption: States are the part of the pattern built so far. Each flip is H or T with chance $\tfrac12$.

screens.question: Solve the three equations and fill in the table.

hints.text: Express $E_{HH}$ and then $E_H$ through $E_0$.
$E_H = \tfrac32 + \tfrac34 E_0$; then $E_0 = 2 + E_H$, so $\tfrac14 E_0 = \tfrac72$ and $E_0 = 14$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each $E$ in terms of $E_0$, then solve for $E_0$.

byKey.r2c1: Write $E_{HH} = 1 + \tfrac12 E_0$ and $E_H = \tfrac32 + \tfrac34 E_0$, then the first equation gives $E_0 = 14$.

explain.text: Back-substitution gives $E_0 = 14$, with 8 left from HH and 12 from H. One, two and three heads take 2, 6 and 14 flips. Each is twice the last, plus 2.

screens.title: A biased coin
screens.prose: Wait for HH with a coin that shows heads with chance $p = \tfrac23$. The same chain gives $E_H = 1 + \tfrac13 E_0$ and $E_0 = 1 + \tfrac23 E_H + \tfrac13 E_0$.

state.caption: States are the part of the pattern built so far. Heads have chance $\tfrac23$ here.

screens.question: What is $E_0$? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: Substitute $E_H = 1 + \tfrac13 E_0$.
$E_0 = 1 + \tfrac23 + \tfrac29 E_0 + \tfrac13 E_0$.
$\tfrac49 E_0 = \tfrac53$, so $E_0 = \tfrac{15}{4}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $E_H$ into the second equation.

byKey.fair: That is the fair coin. With heads at $\tfrac23$ the wait is shorter.
byKey.squared: You squared the wait for one head, $(1/p)^2$. A tail at H restarts you, which adds to that.

explain.text: In general $E_0 = (1 + p)/p^2$, which is 6 at $p = \tfrac12$. At $p = \tfrac23$ it is $\tfrac{15}{4} = 3.75$. As a check, $p = 1$ gives 2 flips, as it must.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose: Every chain here used one rule. The **state** is the longest end of your flips that starts the pattern. For each state $s$, $$E_s = 1 + p\,E_{s_H} + q\,E_{s_T}, \qquad E_{\text{pattern}} = 0,$$ where $s_H$ and $s_T$ are the states after a head and after a tail.
screens.question: Waiting for HTH, you hold HT and flip a T. Which state are you in?

options.why: Your last flip is a T, and HTH starts with H. Nothing you hold starts the pattern.
The T does not extend HT to HTH, so you cannot stay at HT.

feedback.correct: HTT ends in T, and HTH starts with H, so nothing is kept.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the longest end of HTT that begins HTH.

explain.text: The ends of HTT are T, TT and HTT, and none of them begins HTH. So the state is the start. For HTH after HT and a head, you finish instead.

screens.title: Solve HH line by line
screens.prose: Put the HH solution in order, one justified line at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: From H: a head finishes and a tail restarts, so $E_H = 1 + \tfrac12 E_0$.
From the start: a head reaches H and a tail stays, so $E_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_0$.
From H a tail keeps you at H, so $E_H = 2$.

hints.text: Which lines are the two equations?
Lines that start "From H" and "From the start" come first, in either order.
Equations, substitute, solve.

feedback.correct: Two first-step equations, one substitution, one division.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write both equations before you substitute.

byKey.d1: That is the HT chain, where a head keeps you at H. For HH a tail after a head keeps nothing.
byKey.left-out: Both equations, the substitution and the result all belong.
byKey.s3: The substitution needs both equations written first.

explain.text: The first two lines are first-step analysis, one per state. Line 3 removes $E_H$, and line 4 solves for $E_0 = 6$. Say this out loud in an interview: it takes under a minute.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `wait_time(pattern, p)`: the expected flips until an H/T pattern appears, with heads at chance $p$, as an exact `Fraction`. Two helpers are provided. `next_state(pattern, k, flip)` gives the new state, and `solve(A, b)` solves a linear system exactly.
screens.question: Build the first-step equations and solve them.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction

# Provided: next_state(pattern, k, flip) and solve(A, b).


def wait_time(pattern, p=Fraction(1, 2)):
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, each needing an exact `Fraction`. They are HT, HH, HHH, HTH and the one-flip pattern T. Then HH at $p = \tfrac23$, TT at $p = \tfrac35$, and HTTH.

hints.text: One unknown $E_k$ for each $k$ from 0 to $n - 1$ letters held.
Row $k$: $E_k - p\,E_{j_H} - q\,E_{j_T} = 1$, leaving out any $j$ equal to $n$.
Set `A[k][k] += 1`, subtract each chance at its next state below $n$, set `b[k] = 1`, and return `solve(A, b)[0]`.

feedback.correct: The first-step equations solve every pattern exactly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: HH should give 6. Check that a state reaching the full pattern contributes 0, not $E$ of the pattern.
byKey.test-5: A one-flip pattern has one state, the start: $E_0 = 1 + q E_0$, so $E_0 = 1/p$.

explain.text: Each state gives one equation, $E_k = 1 + p\,E_{j_H} + q\,E_{j_T}$, with $E_n = 0$. The solver returns every $E_k$, and the start is $E_0$. HTTH gives 18, because its end H restarts the pattern.

screens.title: Two losing days in a row
screens.prose: A strategy loses on any day with chance 0.4, independently of other days. Its risk limit triggers after two losing days in a row.

state.caption: L is a losing day, chance 0.4; W is any other day, chance 0.6.

screens.question: How many trading days do you expect until the limit triggers? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: A losing day is a head with $p = 0.4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. This is HH with $p = 0.4$.

byKey.squared: You used $1/p^2$. A good day after a loss sends you back to the start, which adds to that.
byKey.fair: That is the fair-coin answer. Losses here have chance 0.4, not 0.5.

explain.text: Two losses in a row is the pattern HH with $p = 0.4$, so $E_0 = 1.4/0.16 = 8.75$ days. A risk manager can quote that before the strategy starts. A daily loss chance of 0.5 would bring it down to 6.

ideas: Track the state: the longest end of your flips that starts the pattern.
First-step analysis: $E_s = 1 + p\,E_{s_H} + q\,E_{s_T}$ for every state, with 0 at the pattern.
A pattern that overlaps itself, like HH, takes longer than one that does not, like HT.

formula.name: Waiting for HH
formula.note: Six flips for a fair coin, against four for HT.

summary.trap: Thinking HH and HT take equally long because each has chance $\tfrac14$ on two flips.

quiz.prose: Flip a fair coin until two tails in a row appear.
quiz.question: How many flips do you expect?

options.why: That is HT. For TT a head at state T sends you back to the start.
That is HHT or HTT. TT is the mirror image of HH.

feedback.correct: TT is HH with the faces swapped: 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap heads and tails in the HH chain.

explain.text: Swapping heads and tails turns TT into HH, and a fair coin does not care which face is which. So $E = 6$.

quiz.prose: Flip a fair coin until HTH appears.
quiz.question: How many flips do you expect?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the states start, H and HT. At H, a head keeps you at H.

byKey.eight: You ignored the overlap. The last H of HTH can start the next try, which changes the equations.

explain.text: With states start, H and HT: $E_{HT} = 1 + \tfrac12 E_0$, $E_H = 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_{HT}$, $E_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_0$. They give $E_{HT} = 6$, $E_H = 8$ and $E_0 = 10$.

quiz.prose: Flip a fair coin until HHT appears.
quiz.question: How many flips do you expect?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At HH, a head keeps you at HH.

byKey.fourteen: That is HHH, where a wrong flip restarts. For HHT a head at HH keeps you at HH.
byKey.six: That is HH, without the final T.

explain.text: From HH a tail finishes and a head keeps you at HH, so $E_{HH} = 2$. Then $E_H = 1 + \tfrac12 E_{HH} + \tfrac12 E_0$ and $E_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 E_H + \tfrac12 E_0$ give $E_0 = 8$.

quiz.prose: A coin shows heads with chance 0.25. The pattern is a single H.
quiz.question: How many flips do you expect until it appears?

byKey.quarter: That is the chance per flip. The wait is its reciprocal.
byKey.two: That is a fair coin. This coin shows heads only one time in four.

explain.text: A pattern of one flip has one state, so $E_0 = 1 + q E_0$ and $E_0 = 1/p = 4$. This is the edge case of first-step analysis.
